DSCP pf writes into every packet of this class's connections, both ways, their two ECN bits left as they came. EF (46) is the usual mark for voice. A mark is fixed when a connection opens: a change reaches new connections. Firewall: Shaper probably sees the mark on uploads only, not measured: pf writes it as a packet comes in on the class's interface, and on a reply as it leaves by it, so a download arriving on the WAN still carries the DSCP it came with.

Firewall: Shaper is read here and never written, and it still shapes on the host: os-xgs-npu keeps every connection an enabled rule of it names with the host, off the hardware. With Follow Firewall: Shaper on (General), what the switch can do of a rule is done in its queues too, at Apply: a queue's weight, against the other queues of its pipe, as a part of every port for a DSCP a class here marks and has a queue for, from a rule on a front port behind the switch - where neither the queue nor its pipe has a mask, the pipe's scheduler shares by weight, no class has a minimum of its own, every switch queue gets a part, and the parts add up to 100 percent at most - and a pipe's bandwidth as a front port's egress limit, where a rule sends everything leaving that port into the pipe and no rule before it on that interface takes part of it first, in the switch's steps of 1 Mbit/s up to 100 Mbit/s and 10 Mbit/s up to 1 Gbit/s. Not measured yet: a part or a limit from a rule here.

IPv4 by default. On an XGS appliance with os-xgs-npu, a marked IPv6 connection stays with the host - its fast path does not write an IPv6 traffic class - so that connection is not forwarded in hardware.

Mark connections of classes switched on with their DSCP, and - on an XGS 3300 whose switch os-xgs-npu sets - give the first two DSCPs their own switch queue, taking those DSCPs off every other connection opening with them, since the switch queues every frame of a DSCP. Off, their rules are gone at the next filter reload and connections opened after it are not marked, and Apply puts the switch back as it found it; classes stay. Apply puts a change into the firewall and the switch.

Matched now, Matched since reload, packets and bytes: what pf counted for the rules of each class. Every filter reload, an Apply among them, starts them again from 0 - packets and bytes too, unless the firewall keeps counters - while connections keep their mark; and a connection two classes match is counted under both, keeping the mark of the lower sequence. Marked now, above, counts each connection pf holds with a mark set coming in, once, whenever it opened, while a class marks. pfctl shows that a mark is set, not which one, so a normalization rule of yours setting any mark on connections coming in is counted too.

Not in pf: class saved and not applied yet, or Traffic Priority off. Written, not loaded: the last filter reload wrote its rules and pf does not hold them. Not placed: OPNsense wrote its rule commented out - an interface not there, an address or a port it could not map.

On an XGS 3300 whose switch os-xgs-npu sets: the part of a full port, in percent, this class's switch queue gets at least. Without minimums the classes in the switch are strict, served before everything else, and can take a whole port; with them their queues are weighted and the rest of the port keeps what is left. Strict and weighted are not mixed: every class with a switch queue has a minimum, or none has. Only the first two DSCPs in the list's order have a queue of their own, and the minimums of the classes switched on add up to 100 at most. The switch has one set of weights for every port in weighted mode, the coprocessor's own uplink among them, so the part is the same on each; queues 1 to 6, which no class takes, get one turn each in it - frames your clients mark themselves (DSCP 8 to 55) wait in those queues on their way into the coprocessor, and when that link is full each queue gets about one turn in a hundred. Not measured yet: whether the switch shares a port by frames or by bytes.

On an XGS 3300 whose switch os-xgs-npu sets: what the switch can do of Firewall: Shaper's rules, done in its queues too - a queue's weight as a part of every port for a DSCP a class here marks and has a queue for, where the queue and its pipe have no mask and the pipe's scheduler shares by weight; and a pipe's bandwidth as a front port's egress limit, in the switch's steps, where a rule sends everything leaving that port into it and no rule before it on that interface takes part of it first. Firewall: Shaper is read, never written, and still shapes on the host. The Firewall: Shaper tab says for each rule what the switch takes and what stays with the host.
Only connections whose first packet arrives with this DSCP - a phone or a game that marks its own traffic, say. Any: whatever they carry. Best Effort (0) cannot be told apart from Any in pf.

Switch queue: on an XGS 3300, every frame the coprocessor sends into its switch waits in queue 0, marked or not; os-xgs-npu picks out two DSCPs there and gives each a queue of its own, on every front port behind the switch at once - the first two in this list's order of the classes that make a rule, IPv4, above Best Effort. The switch picks out every frame with the DSCP, whoever marked it, so a DSCP the classes use in the switch is taken off other traffic: pf sets it to 0 on every other connection opening with it, before the classes mark theirs. A connection that opens without it and whose replies carry it keeps it on the way back - pf fixes a mark when a connection opens. Classes without a minimum are strict: they go before everything else, and can take a whole port. With minimums they are weighted: each keeps at least its part of a full port, and the rest keeps what is left; strict and weighted are not mixed. The front ports on the coprocessor's own MACs - F1 and F2 - are not behind the switch. Measured on an XGS 3300: EF picked out into queue 7; not yet with these classes, nor a minimum held.
The minimums of the classes switched on would add up to more than 100 percent.
